q-80135:
The difference formula for sine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡x-R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
5\operatorname{sin}⁡x-5\operatorname{cos}⁡x=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
5\operatorname{sin}⁡x-5\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=5 \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=5\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ} & =\frac{5}{5} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡ϕ & =1 \\ ϕ & ={45}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-107574:
The sum formula for sine gives

$$
\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+ϕ) & =R(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) \\  & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡x+R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by writing the given expression in the amplitude-phase form

$$
\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\operatorname{cos}⁡x=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+ϕ),
$$

we get the following identity:

$$
\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\operatorname{cos}⁡x=(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ we get the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ=\sqrt{5} \\ R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=2\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing the second equation by the first, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ} & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡ϕ & =\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5} \\ ϕ & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5}) \\ ϕ & ≈0.730\,\text{rad}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

Now, we find the amplitude $R.$ Squaring the first and the second equations of the system and adding the results together, we get: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ+{R}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ & =(\sqrt{5})^{2}+{2}^{2} \\ {R}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡ϕ+{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ) & =5+4 \\ {R}^{2} & =9 \\ R & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we only consider the positive root since $R>0.$

Finally, we can write the initial expression in amplitude-phase form as follows:

$$
\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\operatorname{cos}⁡x≈3\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+0.730)
$$

q-17128:
We notice that the point $P$ is described using polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ where

$$
r=2,\,\theta =\frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =2\cdot 0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =2(-1) \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $(0,-2).$

q-120598:
First, since $A$ has polar coordinates $(2,{240}^{∘}),$ we must have $r=2.$ Also, since the points $A$ and $B$ both lie on a circle of radius $2,$ the $r$-coordinate of $B$ must also be $2.$

Notice that one must traverse the circle clockwise to move from the point $A$ to point $B.$ Since the $\theta $-coordinate of $A$ is ${240}^{∘},$ the $\theta $-coordinate of $B$ must be

$$
{\theta }_{B}={240}^{∘}-{195}^{∘}={45}^{∘}.
$$

So, the polar coordinates of $B$ are $(2,{45}^{∘})$

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡({45}^{∘}) \\  & =2(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡({45}^{∘}) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2}).$

q-8683:
First, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})=\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\frac{\pi }{4}$ lies inside the required domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}=\frac{\pi }{4}.$

Our first solution lies in the first quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Since $\operatorname{cos}⁡x>0,$ the second solution must lie in the fourth quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{4}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13968930/assets/caa6662d8349751e35bcb1af4196ad043b66ea64f21805eb6ca9b14435d38458.png)

A second solution $X$ lies in the $4$th quadrant, and we can find it using the reference angle, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}X & =2\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =2\pi -\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

However, this value is not in the required domain. To get a second solution that's within the required domain, we simply subtract $2\pi $ from $X:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =X-2\pi  \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{4}-2\pi  \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $x=-\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4}.$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}{x}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot (-\frac{\pi }{4})=-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{16}.
$$

q-72838:
First, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{4}{7})=0.962\,550…≈0.962\,6\end{aligned}
$$

Since $0.962\,6$ lies inside the specified domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}=0.962\,6.$

Our first solution lies in the first quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}=0.962\,6.$ Since $\operatorname{cos}⁡x>0,$ the second solution must lie in the fourth quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}=0.962\,6.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13968930/assets/b2cd7e76526632d8507ba484246a560829882e7f10d9814f01593f7a48d9a2ac.png)

Since the second solution ${x}_{2}$ lies in the $4$th quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =2\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =2\pi -0.962\,6 \\  & =5.320\,6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}{x}_{2}≈0.962\,6\cdot 5.320\,6≈5.1
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

q-278483:
On the interval $(-2,8),$ we can choose a test point ${x}_{1}=0.$ Then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2 & =0+2=(+), \\ x-8 & =0-8=(-), \\ (x+2)(x-8) & =(+)\times (-)=(-),\end{aligned}
$$

and we fill in the table as follows:

|  | $(-\infty ,-2)$ | $(-2,8)$ | $(8,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x+2$ | $-$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| $x-8$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ |
| $(x+2)(x-8)$ | $+$ | $-$ | $+$ |

q-115426:
First, let's factor the left-hand side of the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+13x & <0 \\ x(x+13) & <0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the roots of the corresponding equation $x(x+13)=0.$ The roots are $x=-13$ and $x=0,$ and they split the number line into the $3$ intervals $(-\infty ,-13),$ $(-13,0),$ and $(0,\infty ).$

Now, we construct a sign table with the list of the intervals on the top and the list of factors on the left. Filling in the sign table using the usual method, we get the following result:

|  | $(-\infty ,-13)$ | $(-13,0)$ | $(0,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x+13$ | $-$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| $x$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ |
| $x(x+13)$ | $(-)\cdot (-)=+$ | $(+)\cdot (-)=-$ | $(+)\cdot (+)=+$ |

Finally, to solve the quadratic inequality $x(x+13)<0,$ we look at the bottom row to find out where the expression $x(x+13)$ is negative.

We see that the expression is negative on the interval $(-13,0).$ 

Therefore, we conclude that ${x}^{2}+13x<0$ for all $x\in (-13,0).$

q-27068:
First, let's factor the left-hand side of the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-3x-10 & >0 \\ (x+2)(x-5) & >0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the roots of the corresponding equation $(x+2)(x-5)=0.$ The roots are $x=-2$ and $x=5,$ and they split the number line into the $3$ intervals $(-\infty ,-2),$ $(-2,5),$ and $(5,\infty ).$

Now, we construct a sign table with the list of the intervals on the top and the list of factors on the left. Filling in the sign table using the usual method, we get the following result:

|  | $(-\infty ,-2)$ | $(-2,5)$ | $(5,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x+2$ | $-$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| $x-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ |
| $(x+2)(x-5)$ | $(-)\cdot (-)=+$ | $(+)\cdot (-)=-$ | $(+)\cdot (+)=+$ |

Finally, to solve the quadratic inequality $(x+2)(x-5)>0,$ we look at the bottom row to find out where the expression $(x+2)(x-5)$ is positive.

We see that the expression is positive on the intervals $(-\infty ,-2)\cup (5,\infty ).$ 

Therefore, we conclude that ${x}^{2}-3x-10>0$ for all $x\in (-\infty ,-2)\cup (5,\infty ).$

q-27071:
First, let's factor the left-hand side of the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-3x-36 & \le 0 \\ 3({x}^{2}-x-12) & \le 0 \\ 3(x+3)(x-4) & \le 0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the roots of the corresponding equation $(x+3)(x-4)=0.$ The roots are $x=-3$ and $x=4,$ and they split the number line into the $3$ subintervals $(-\infty ,-3),$ $(-3,4),$ and $(4,\infty ).$

Now, we construct a sign table with the list of the intervals on the top and the list of factors on the left. Filling in the sign table using the usual method, we get the following result:

|  | $(-\infty ,-3)$ | $(-3,4)$ | $(4,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x+3$ | $-$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| $x-4$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ |
| $(x+3)(x-4)$ | $(-)\cdot (-)=+$ | $(+)\cdot (-)=-$ | $(+)\cdot (+)=+$ |

Finally, to solve the quadratic inequality $3(x+3)(x-4)\le 0,$ we look at the bottom row to find out where the expression $3(x+3)(x-4)$ is zero or negative.

We see that the expression is negative on the interval $(-3,4).$ Also, we know that the expression equals $0$ at the points $x=-3$ and $x=4.$

Therefore, we conclude that $(x+3)(x-4)\le 0$ for all $x\in [-3,4].$

q-116200:
First, we rewrite the given inequality so that the right-hand side equals zero. Then, we factor the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{x}^{2}+\frac{3}{5}x & \ge 2 \\ \frac{1}{5}{x}^{2}+\frac{3}{5}x-2 & \ge 0 \\ \frac{1}{5}({x}^{2}+3x-10) & \ge 0 \\ \frac{1}{5}(x+5)(x-2) & \ge 0 \\ (x+5)(x-2) & \ge 0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the roots of the corresponding equation $(x+5)(x-2).$ The roots are $x=-5$ and $x=2,$ and they split the number line into the $3$ subintervals $(-\infty ,-5),$ $(-5,2),$ and $(2,\infty ).$

Now, we construct a sign table with the list of the intervals on the top and the list of factors on the left. Filling in the sign table using the usual method, we get the following result:

|  | $(-\infty ,-5)$ | $(-5,2)$ | $(2,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x+5$ | $-$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| $x-2$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ |
| $(x+5)(x-2)$ | $(-)\cdot (-)=+$ | $(+)\cdot (-)=-$ | $(+)\cdot (+)=+$ |

Finally, to solve the quadratic inequality $(x+5)(x-2)\ge 0,$ we look at the bottom row to find out where the expression $(x+5)(x-2)$ is zero or positive.

We see that the expression is positive on the intervals $(-\infty ,-5)$ and $(2,\infty ).$ Also, we know that the expression equals $0$ at the points $x=-5$ and $x=2.$

Therefore, we conclude that $\frac{1}{5}{x}^{2}+\frac{3}{5}x\ge 2$ for all $x\in (-\infty ,-5]\cup [2,\infty ).$

q-74653:
First, we set up the fraction:

$$
\frac{5-2\text{i}}{3\text{i}}
$$

The denominator is the imaginary number $3\text{i}.$ Note that this can be written as $0+3\text{i},$ so the conjugate is $0-3\text{i},$ or simply $-3\text{i}.$

So, we multiply both the numerator and the denominator by $-3\text{i},$ so that the denominator turns into a real number:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{{z}_{1}}{{z}_{2}} & =\frac{5-2\text{i}}{3\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{5-2\text{i}}{3\text{i}}\cdot \frac{-3\text{i}}{-3\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{-15\text{i}+6{\text{i}}^{2}}{-9{\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-15\text{i}+6(-1)}{-9(-1)} \\  & =\frac{-6-15\text{i}}{9}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the denominator is a real number, we can write the complex number in the form $a+b\text{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{-6-15\text{i}}{9}=-\frac{6}{9}-\frac{15}{9}\text{i}=-\frac{2}{3}-\frac{5}{3}\text{i}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

q-7175:
First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{5t-10}{t}) \\  & =\frac{10}{{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

When $t=2,$ the velocity is

$$
v(2)=\frac{10}{(2)^{2}}=\frac{10}{4}=2.5.
$$

Therefore, the speed is $|2.5|=2.5\,\text{cm/s}.$

q-72252:
Remember that the general equation of an ellipse centered at $(h,k)$ with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

Here, the ellipse is centered at $(-2,-2),$ the horizontal radius has length $a=3,$ and the vertical radius has length $b=4.$ Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{b}^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-(-2))^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{(y-(-2))^{2}}{{4}^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{(x+2)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{16} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$
